content: These methods are outlined in public water system guidelines and compliance technology lists, such as those for the Surface Water Treatment Rule and Total Coliform Rule. For example, in New Zealand, the 2022 Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules mandate specific treatment requirements for all drinking water supplies, except those serving a single household. Supplies serving 101 to 500 people must filter all water through media, membrane, or cartridge systems, treat it with ultraviolet disinfection, and chlorinate it. Alternative compliance options, known as acceptable solutions, are also available for certain water sources, such as roof water, springs, and boreholes, provided they are implemented in full. In Ghana, the Ghana Standards Authority introduced a standard in 2022 for household water treatment (HWT) products and technologies, focusing on pathogen removal. This standard defines performance classifications based on log reduction criteria for bacteria, viruses, and protozoa, and specifies testing methods, labeling, and packaging requirements. In Finland, the Health Protection Act of 1994 requires water supply operators, including those managing small supplies, to undergo competency examinations every five years. These exams cover water treatment technology, monitoring, legislation, and hygiene. Operators of supplies serving more than 50 people or providing over 10 m³ of water daily are required to participate, while smaller supplies may do so voluntarily. This system has improved staff training, knowledge, and operational practices. In the occupied Palestinian territory, the Water Sector Regulatory Council oversees over 300 water and sanitation service providers, including small supplies. It has introduced material safety standards for products in contact with drinking water, aligning with international and regional standards. A phased implementation approach, supported by monitoring and collaboration with health and water authorities, helps suppliers progressively upgrade their systems to meet these standards. In Wales, private water supplies, defined as those not connected to public mains, have been subject to risk assessments since 2010 under the Private Water Supplies (Wales) Regulations. This proactive risk management has significantly improved microbial water quality, with E. coli contamination in samples decreasing from over 20% in 2010 to less than 7% in 2022. In the Asia-Pacific region, an evaluation of water safety plans (WSPs) in 12 countries between 2014 and 2016 showed significant improvements in operations and management practices at 93 out of 99 water supply sites. These improvements included better monitoring, emergency response plans, maintenance schedules, and consumer education. In Germany, the revised EU Drinking Water Directive requires risk assessment and management for water supplies serving at least 500 people or providing 100 m³ of water daily. Smaller supplies are also encouraged to adopt risk management practices, with inspections of catchment areas required annually to identify and address risks to water quality. In the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, water safety plan requirements introduced in 2014 allowed urban suppliers five years and rural suppliers ten years to comply. This extended timeline enabled health authorities to provide training and support to the more numerous rural suppliers. In Madagascar, the Tatirano Social Enterprise collaborates with the Ministry of Water to implement the national Water Code. It prioritizes proactive inspection and maintenance of rainwater harvesting systems in remote communities, incorporating risk management principles into training for local field agents. In Bhutan, WSPs have been mandatory since 2016. Templates tailored to the capacities of municipal and community-managed supplies have been developed. Municipal supplies use electronic templates, while community supplies use simpler, paper-based templates completed during workshops. In Finland, WSP implementation is required for all drinking water suppliers, with requirements varying by supply size. Larger supplies use a web-based tool for comprehensive risk management, while smaller supplies may use simplified checklists. In Vanuatu, community water suppliers must implement drinking water safety and security plans. Improvement needs identified in these plans can be funded through the government’s Capital Assistance Programme, with prioritization based on risk and vulnerability. In Cambodia, water safety planning is used to enhance the climate resilience of rural drinking water supplies. Teuk Saat 1001, a local NGO, operates water treatment kiosks staffed by trained entrepreneurs, contributing to the government’s goal of universal access to improved water supplies by 2025.
